To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The scientific value of simulations can be increased by careful planning and algorithmic optimizations that are specific to a given application, and that are made as our understanding of that application evolves.”

1) The scientific outcome of large-scale simulations can be improved by a factor of up to 10x by optimizing the algorithms, 2) The optimizations can be done by the end users, and do not require any special privileges or access to the source code of the simulation codes, and 3) The optimizations are not trivial and require a detailed understanding of the simulation algorithms and the physical processes being simulated.

the scientific outcome of large simulations is maximized by: 1) using the largest available computing platform, 2) using a modular code that is well-structured and has a wide user base, and 3) using a simulation strategy that is informed by a deep understanding of the physics of the problem and the algorithms that are being used.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pragmatic optimizations for better scientific use of the largest supercomputers available.
the pragmatic optimizations required for the efficient use of the largest supercomputers, in order to maximize their scientific return.
the pragmatic aspects of using large HPC platforms to run simulations that can provide scientific insight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single best way of running simulations on large supercomputing resources; rather, a number of pragmatic approaches are necessary to maximize the scientific return.

the current HPC systems, while providing a great deal of computational power, still require a significant amount of optimization to be able to provide the most scientific return for the computational resources used.
the scientific utilization of large HPC resources is challenging, and requires a combination of careful planning and on-the-fly optimizations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the simulations are computationally demanding, but the optimizations and tradeoffs have been made in a manner that allows for scientific progress.

we have found that the best scientific outcome from large-scale simulations on HPC platforms requires an iterative process, in which the scientific objectives and the simulation algorithms are continuously re-evaluated and optimized.
the simulation results have been extremely successful, with a large number of scientific publications and conference presentations already produced, and many more in preparation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the optimization of simulations for large-scale platforms is an ongoing, multi-step process that requires a deep understanding of both the physics and the algorithms, as well as a good understanding of the available resources.
, while the scientific outcome of large-scale HPC simulations can be improved by careful planning and optimization, it is important not to lose sight of the scientific goals.
the scientific value of simulations can be maximized only through close interaction between the code developers and the users.
